notes.h: What pollution is and where it occurs
notes.b: Pollution is a problem caused by people, and it can be small or enormous in scale. Knowing how to define it, classify it and place it on a scale lets you tackle any pollution question.
points: Pollution is the release by human activity of substances or energy (heat, noise, light) into the environment in amounts that harm living things, health or property. Harm is what makes a release pollution.
Types of pollution: air, water (fresh and marine), land and soil, noise and visual. For example, oil in the sea is water pollution and a motorway's roar is noise pollution.
Scales: local (one river or town), national (a country's water quality) and global (the whole atmosphere or ocean). The scale tells you how many people and places are affected.

Transboundary pollution (pollution that crosses national borders) means the place it harms may be far from its source. Acid rain, rain made acidic by gases from burning fuels, is the European example, taught in the note Burning fossil fuels and using alternative energy sources.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask you to name one example of environmental pollution caused by economic activity, then give its causes, effects and how it could be reduced. Make your chosen example stand alone with all three.

notes.h: Point and diffuse sources of pollution
notes.b: Pollution can be traced back to its source in two ways, depending on whether it leaves from one spot or from many. This matters because a single outlet is easier to find and control than thousands of small ones.
points: Point sources come from one identifiable place, such as a factory pipe or a sewage outfall (the pipe where sewage enters a river or the sea).
Diffuse sources come from many places at once, such as runoff (rainwater washing substances off the land) from many farms, or traffic.
Economic activities that pollute include agriculture, manufacturing, energy generation, transport, mining, tourism, households and urban waste.

notes.h: The natural and enhanced greenhouse effect
notes.b: Global warming is the main global-scale example of pollution. It starts with a natural process that human activity has strengthened.
points: The natural greenhouse effect: greenhouse gases (gases in the atmosphere that trap heat) let incoming short-wave solar radiation through but absorb outgoing long-wave radiation (heat given off by the earth), which keeps the earth habitable.
The enhanced greenhouse effect: human activity adds greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, which trap more heat and so warm the planet further.

notes.b: Each greenhouse gas has its own human sources, and many of them are economic activities. Knowing which activity gives which gas lets you explain the causes of warming.
points: CO2 (carbon dioxide) comes from burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), deforestation (clearing forests, which removes trees that absorb CO2) and cement production.
Methane comes from cattle and sheep, rice paddies, landfill (rubbish buried in the ground) and gas leaks.
Nitrous oxide comes from nitrogen fertilisers and slurry (liquid animal manure).
CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, man-made gases) and other fluorinated gases are also greenhouse gases.
notes.tip: The ozone hole is not the cause of global warming. CFCs are greenhouse gases as well as ozone destroyers, but the two problems have different mechanisms and different treaties (Montreal vs Kyoto/Paris).

notes.b: Scientists measure warming in several independent ways, and they all point the same way. Each measurement below is a piece of evidence you can quote.
points: Atmospheric CO2 was about 280 ppm (parts per million) before the Industrial Revolution. It passed 400 ppm in the mid-2010s and was over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s. These readings are measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, which has recorded them since 1958.
Global average surface temperature has risen by about 1.1 to 1.2 °C since the late 1800s (IPCC, the UN's climate science panel).
2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels (Copernicus, the EU's Earth observation programme).
Arctic summer sea ice has shrunk by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979.
Global sea level rose by about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018 (IPCC).
Glaciers (large masses of ice on land) are retreating worldwide, which is a visible sign that temperatures are rising.
notes.tip: Evidence for global warming needs facts: rising CO2 concentration, rising temperature, record years, retreating glaciers, shrinking Arctic sea ice and rising sea level. Do not give temperature or sea-level projections for 2100.

notes.b: A warmer atmosphere changes oceans, ice, weather and ecosystems, and these changes harm people and wildlife. The effects are worst for places that are low-lying or already vulnerable.
points: Sea-level rise, from thermal expansion of seawater (water expands as it warms) and melting land ice, threatens low-lying countries and deltas: Bangladesh (the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta), the Maldives, Tuvalu and Kiribati.
More intense heatwaves, droughts, floods and storms. The Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) has suffered droughts.
Glacier retreat threatens water supplies, because many places depend on meltwater from glaciers.
Coral bleaching (corals losing their colour and dying when seas get too warm): the Great Barrier Reef, Australia, has suffered repeated mass bleaching since the late 1990s.
Species shifts and extinctions, crop failures in vulnerable regions, and climate refugees (people forced to leave their homes because of climate change).
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks for one negative impact of CO2 emissions. Pick one effect, such as sea-level rise threatening Bangladesh or the Maldives, and explain it.

notes.h: Global warming in Ireland: temperature and effects
notes.b: Ireland is not exempt from global warming. Its temperature has risen, and the effects are felt on land, at the coast and at sea.
points: Ireland's average temperature has risen by about 0.9 °C since 1900 (EPA and Met Éireann, the national weather service).
Warmer temperatures bring wetter winters and more flooding, a risk of summer drought, stronger storms and coastal erosion (the sea wearing away the coast).
Effects also include changes to farming and to marine species, and a threat to low-lying coastal towns.
Storm Éowyn, in January 2025, caused record damage and power cuts.

notes.b: Ireland's emissions come mainly from a few sectors, and farming dominates. This is why so many Irish climate measures target agriculture.
points: Agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, the largest share, mainly methane and nitrous oxide from cattle, slurry and fertiliser.
Transport, mainly fuel burned by vehicles, is the next largest source, at about a fifth of emissions (EPA, early 2020s), followed by energy.
Ireland's emissions per person are high for an EU country, which is largely because of its large farming sector.
notes.tip: Do not use figures from past-paper emissions charts in your own notes. Learn the order: agriculture first, then transport, then energy.

notes.b: Warming is a global problem, so governments have tried to answer it through international agreements. Each one built on the one before.
points: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was agreed at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.

The Kyoto Protocol, agreed in 1997 and in force from 2005, set legally binding cuts for developed countries only. The USA never ratified it (it signed but did not formally approve it), so it was not a full party.
The Paris Agreement, 2015, aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Each country sets its own national plan (nationally determined contribution).
Countries meet every year at COP meetings (conferences of the countries that signed the UNFCCC). COP30 was held at Belém, Brazil, in November 2025.
notes.tip: The USA signed but never ratified Kyoto. Do not say it was a full Kyoto party.

notes.h: EU and Irish responses to global warming
notes.b: The EU and Ireland have turned the global agreements into laws, targets and charges. Together they put a price on emissions and set deadlines for cutting them.
points: The EU Emissions Trading System began in 2005. Power stations and heavy industry must hold an allowance (a permit) for each tonne of CO2 they emit, which gives them a cost reason to cut emissions.
The European Green Deal (2019) aims for a climate-neutral EU by 2050 (no net emissions). Its Fit for 55 package aims to cut net emissions by at least 55% by 2030, compared with 1990.
Ireland's Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 requires a 51% cut in emissions by 2030, compared with 2018, and net zero by 2050.
Sectoral ceilings (limits on each sector's emissions, set in 2022) require agriculture to cut its emissions by 25% by 2030.
An Irish carbon tax (a charge on fuels based on their CO2) was introduced in 2010 and is rising in stages towards €100 a tonne by 2030.
The Climate Action Plan aims to retrofit (upgrade with insulation and heating) 500,000 homes to a B2 energy rating by 2030, and includes renewables, electric vehicles and measures for agriculture.
notes.tip: Questions on reducing greenhouse gas emissions can ask for two ways. Pick two of these measures and say what each does.

notes.h: How individuals and communities can reduce emissions
notes.b: Governments cannot cut emissions alone, because homes, transport and food are all household choices. Everyday changes add up.
points: Improve energy efficiency and insulate homes, so less fuel is burned for heating.
Use public transport, cycling and walking in place of car journeys, so fewer fossil fuels are burned.
Reduce food waste, because rotting food in landfill gives off methane.
Switch to renewable heating, because it does not burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas, so it gives off less CO2.

notes.h: Agricultural water pollution: causes and eutrophication
notes.b: Agricultural water pollution is the Irish national case study of water pollution. Nutrients meant to grow crops end up in rivers and lakes, where they set off a chain of events called eutrophication.
points: Cause: nitrogen and phosphorus from slurry, manure and chemical fertilisers wash off fields into rivers and lakes, especially after heavy rain or when spread on wet or frozen ground. Silage effluent (liquid from stored grass) and sewage from towns and septic tanks (private sewage tanks) add more.
Eutrophication (water becoming overloaded with nutrients): the nutrients feed rapid algal growth, forming algal blooms (dense layers of algae).
When the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and other life suffocate in fish kills.
The water turns green and smells. Some blue-green algae are toxic.
notes.tip: For the Ordinary Level and Higher Level questions on this, give the cause, then the effects, then how it could be reduced. Get the order of eutrophication right: nutrients, algal bloom, algae die, bacteria use up oxygen, fish die.

notes.b: Polluted water harms wildlife first, and then the people and businesses that rely on clean water.
points: Loss of fish and other wildlife, such as in a fish kill, and damage to angling and tourism, because few people visit or fish in green, smelly water.
Drinking water needs costly treatment, and nitrates (nitrogen compounds from fertiliser) contaminate groundwater (water held underground).
Coastal waters, including estuaries (where rivers meet the sea), are affected by algal mats, because rivers carry the nutrients downstream.

notes.b: The EPA, which monitors water quality, shows that pollution is a national problem and not only a local one. Farming is the main pressure.
points: An EPA assessment for 2016 to 2021 found that only about half of Ireland's rivers, lakes and estuaries were in good or high ecological status.
Agriculture is the most common pressure on water quality, followed by urban wastewater (sewage from towns), because fertiliser and slurry wash into streams.
Milk quotas (limits on how much milk farms could produce) were abolished on 1 April 2015. The dairy herd then grew strongly, especially in the south and east, and raised nitrogen levels there.

notes.h: Case study: Lough Neagh algal bloom, 2023
notes.b: Lough Neagh is a real example of eutrophication, and the 2023 bloom shows the processes above in action. Treat it as a single event, and do not claim it has been solved.
points: Lough Neagh, Northern Ireland, is the largest lake on the island of Ireland. In summer 2023 a huge toxic blue-green algal bloom covered much of it.
The bloom was blamed on nutrient pollution from farm runoff, sewage and septic tanks, together with warm weather and invasive zebra mussels that clear the water, letting more light reach the algae.
Lough Neagh supplies a large share of Northern Ireland's drinking water, so a toxic bloom threatens a key water supply.
notes.tip: Lough Neagh is in Northern Ireland and is the largest lake on the island. Lough Corrib is the largest in the Republic.

notes.b: Reducing the pollution means keeping nutrients on the land and out of water. Most of the rules limit when, where and how much farmers spread.
points: The EU Nitrates Directive (1991) and Ireland's Nitrates Action Programme set closed periods each winter when slurry and fertiliser may not be spread, because rain would wash them straight into rivers.

The Nitrates Action Programme also limits nitrogen per hectare, requires slurry storage, and requires buffer strips (strips of vegetation) beside watercourses, which trap nutrients before they reach the water.
The EU Water Framework Directive (2000) aims for good status for all waters, which gives countries a target to work towards.
Other measures: upgrading urban wastewater treatment, EPA monitoring of water quality, and farm advisory programmes.

notes.b: Oil in the sea comes from accidents and from deliberate or careless releases. It is a global pollution problem because oil is moved and drilled for all over the world.
points: Tanker accidents, drilling blow-outs (uncontrolled releases of oil from a well), illegal tank washing at sea, and pipeline leaks release oil into the sea.

notes.b: The Exxon Valdez is a tanker accident that caused huge damage to a wild coast and led to a change in law. Remember it is in Alaska, not the Gulf of Mexico.
points: The tanker ran aground on Bligh Reef, Prince William Sound, Alaska, on 24 March 1989.
About 11 million US gallons (about 37,000 tonnes) of crude oil were spilled, and about 2,000 km of coastline was oiled.
Hundreds of thousands of seabirds and thousands of sea otters were killed, and the herring fishery collapsed.
The response was the US Oil Pollution Act 1990, which required double-hulled tankers (tankers with two layers of steel, so a hit is less likely to leak) in US waters.

notes.b: The Prestige shows that a tanker accident can damage the coasts of several countries and the fishing that depends on them.
points: The single-hulled tanker Prestige broke in two and sank off Galicia, north-west Spain, in November 2002. It spilled tens of thousands of tonnes of heavy fuel oil.
Oil reached the Costa da Morte and the coasts of Spain, Portugal and France. Galician shellfish and fishing industries were closed for months.
The disaster sped up the EU's phase-out of single-hulled tankers, because a single hull is more likely to leak after damage.

notes.b: Deepwater Horizon is an example of oil pollution from drilling, and not from a tanker. It is in the Gulf of Mexico.
points: The Deepwater Horizon rig (an offshore drilling platform), operated by BP, exploded on 20 April 2010 in the Gulf of Mexico. Eleven workers were killed.
About 4.9 million barrels of oil were spilled.

notes.h: Effects, clean-up and prevention of oil spills
notes.b: Whatever the cause, oil spills have similar effects, and the same responses are used in each. Know the effects first, then the clean-up and the prevention.
points: Effects: oiled seabirds and mammals, smothered shorelines, fishing bans and lost tourism, because beaches and catches are unusable.
Clean-up: booms (floating barriers) to contain the oil, skimmers (machines that scoop oil off the surface) to remove it, and dispersants (chemicals) to break it up.
Prevention: double-hulled tankers, and routing ships away from coasts, so that any accident happens far from the shore.

notes.h: Plastic and waste pollution: causes and effects
notes.b: Plastic is cheap and lasts a very long time, which is why it is a problem once it is thrown away. It pollutes at local and global scale.
points: Causes: single-use packaging that is thrown away after one use, litter, illegal dumping and landfill (burying rubbish in the ground).
Plastics take hundreds of years to break down, and they fragment into microplastics (tiny pieces of plastic).
Effects: litter in towns and countryside, and wildlife entangled in or eating plastic, which can injure or kill animals.
Ocean garbage patches: the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a large area of the North Pacific where floating plastic collects in an ocean gyre (a large circling ocean current).
Microplastics enter food chains, as animals eat them. Landfill produces leachate (polluted liquid that drains from rubbish) and methane.

notes.h: Irish responses to plastic and waste
notes.b: Ireland has tried to cut plastic and waste by putting a price on it, by rewarding returns, and by ranking how waste should be handled.
points: The plastic bag levy (a charge on each bag) was introduced in March 2002 at 15 cent a bag, raised to 22 cent in 2007. Plastic bag use fell by over 90% almost at once, and the money funds environmental projects.
The Deposit Return Scheme (Re-turn) began on 1 February 2024 for plastic drinks bottles and cans.
The waste hierarchy ranks reduce, reuse, recycle, recover and dispose. The EPA licenses waste facilities.
The Dublin Waste-to-Energy incinerator at Poolbeg (a plant that burns waste to make energy) has operated since 2017.

notes.b: Ozone depletion is a different problem from global warming, with a different cause and a different treaty. It is also a success story.
points: CFCs, from aerosols, fridges and air conditioning, destroy stratospheric ozone (the ozone in the upper atmosphere), which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
British Antarctic Survey scientists reported the Antarctic ozone hole (a thin area in the ozone layer over Antarctica) in 1985.
More ultraviolet radiation causes skin cancer and eye cataracts, and damages plankton and crops.
The Montreal Protocol, agreed in 1987, phased out CFCs. Every UN member state has ratified it, and it is often cited as the most successful global environmental agreement.
The Antarctic ozone layer is expected to recover to 1980 levels around the 2060s (UN assessment, 2023).
notes.tip: The ozone hole is not the cause of global warming. The treaty for ozone is Montreal, and Kyoto and Paris deal with warming.

notes.b: Pollution also occurs closer to home, from traffic, old mines and large structures. Each of these is a local example.
points: Air pollution in towns: traffic produces nitrogen dioxide and fine particles. Home burning of solid fuel adds smoke, which is why smoke-free zones exist in some towns (see the note Burning fossil fuels and using alternative energy sources for smoke-free zones).
Mining pollution: acid mine drainage (acidic water flowing out of old mines) from old copper mines at Avoca, Co. Wicklow, discolours and pollutes the Avoca River.
Noise and visual pollution (unwanted sound and ugly views) from airports, motorways, quarries, wind farms and pylons.

keyTerms.definition: The release by human activity of substances or energy into the environment in amounts that harm living things, health or property.
A pollution source from one identifiable place, such as a factory pipe or sewage outfall.
A pollution source spread over many places, such as runoff from many farms.
The extra warming caused by human-added greenhouse gases trapping more heat in the atmosphere.
The enrichment of water by nutrients, which causes algal growth and then oxygen loss as the algae decay.
A rapid growth of algae in water, often toxic when blue-green algae are involved.
Tiny fragments of plastic that enter water, soil and food chains.
The destruction of stratospheric ozone, mainly by CFCs, which lets more harmful ultraviolet radiation reach the Earth.
Polluted liquid that drains from landfill and can contaminate water.

questions.prompt: Examine one example of environmental pollution at a global scale.
questions.model: Global warming is caused by the enhanced greenhouse effect. The natural greenhouse effect keeps the earth habitable, but human activity adds greenhouse gases. CO2 comes from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and cement production; methane from cattle and sheep, rice paddies, landfill and gas leaks; nitrous oxide from nitrogen fertilisers and slurry; and CFCs. Evidence includes CO2 rising from about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s, measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii; global temperature up about 1.1 to 1.2 °C since the late 1800s; 2024 as the warmest year on record; shrinking Arctic sea ice; retreating glaciers; and sea level up about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018. Global effects include sea-level rise threatening Bangladesh, the Maldives, Tuvalu and Kiribati; more intense heatwaves, droughts, floods and storms; coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef; species extinctions; and crop failures and climate refugees. In Ireland, temperatures have risen by about 0.9 °C since 1900, bringing wetter winters, more flooding, stronger storms and coastal erosion. Agriculture is the largest source of Irish emissions. Internationally, the UNFCCC of 1992 was followed by the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, which bound only developed countries, and the Paris Agreement of 2015, which asks each country to set its own plan. In the EU, the Emissions Trading System began in 2005, and the Green Deal and Fit for 55 aim for a 55% cut by 2030. Ireland's Climate Act 2021 requires a 51% cut by 2030 and net zero by 2050, and a carbon tax has applied since 2010. Individuals can reduce emissions through energy efficiency, insulation, public transport, cycling, less food waste and renewable heating.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one example of environmental pollution caused by economic activity. (ii) Explain its causes and effects. (iii) Describe how it could be reduced.
questions.model: (i) Agricultural water pollution in Ireland. (ii) Causes: nitrogen and phosphorus from slurry, manure and chemical fertilisers wash off fields into rivers and lakes, especially after heavy rain or when spread on wet or frozen ground. The nutrients cause eutrophication: algae grow rapidly, form blooms, and then die, and the bacteria that decompose them use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate. The water turns green, smells, and may contain toxic blue-green algae. Effects: loss of fish and wildlife, damage to angling and tourism, costly treatment of drinking water, nitrates in groundwater, and affected estuaries. The EPA found in 2016 to 2021 that only about half of Ireland's rivers, lakes and estuaries were in good or high status, and agriculture is the most common pressure. In summer 2023 a toxic blue-green algal bloom covered much of Lough Neagh, the largest lake on the island of Ireland, blamed on farm runoff, sewage and septic tanks. (iii) Reduction: the EU Nitrates Directive of 1991 and Ireland's Nitrates Action Programme set closed periods each winter when slurry and fertiliser may not be spread, limit nitrogen per hectare, require slurry storage and buffer strips beside watercourses. The EU Water Framework Directive of 2000 aims for good status for all waters. Urban wastewater treatment is being upgraded, the EPA monitors water quality, and farm advisory programmes help farmers comply.

questions.prompt: Describe the causes and effects of marine oil pollution and how it can be reduced.
questions.model: Marine oil pollution is caused by tanker accidents, drilling blow-outs, illegal tank washing at sea and pipeline leaks. The Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, on 24 March 1989, spilling about 37,000 tonnes of crude oil and oiling about 2,000 km of coastline. Hundreds of thousands of seabirds and thousands of sea otters were killed and the herring fishery collapsed. The response was the US Oil Pollution Act 1990, requiring double-hulled tankers in US waters. The Prestige, a single-hulled tanker, broke in two and sank off Galicia in November 2002, spilling tens of thousands of tonnes of heavy fuel oil. Oil reached the Costa da Morte and the coasts of Spain, Portugal and France, and Galician fishing was closed for months, which sped up the EU phase-out of single-hulled tankers. The Deepwater Horizon exploded in the Gulf of Mexico on 20 April 2010, killing 11 workers and spilling about 4.9 million barrels. Effects of oil spills include oiled seabirds and mammals, smothered shorelines, fishing bans and lost tourism. Clean-up uses booms, skimmers and dispersants, while prevention relies on double-hulled tankers and routing ships away from coasts.
